1.description: This slide introduces two definitions fundamental to convex analysis within the context of Linear Programming and Optimization Techniques.  Definition 1 formally defines a convex set $S$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$:  a set is convex if, for any two points $z_1$ and $z_2$ within the set, the line segment connecting them ($tz_1 + (1-t)z_2$ where $0 < t < 1$) is entirely contained within the set.  Definition 2 defines a convex combination of $n$ points $z_1, z_2, \dots, z_n$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$ as a weighted sum $t_1 z_1 + t_2 z_2 + \dots + t_n z_n$, where the weights $t_i$ are non-negative and sum to 1 ($\sum_i t_i = 1$). The accompanying figures illustrate convex combinations in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^3$, showing how points are combined to form new points within the convex hull.

2.description: This slide presents Theorem 10.1, which states that a set $S$ is convex if and only if it contains all convex combinations of its points. The proof is outlined, focusing on one direction of the implication. It starts by assuming that $S$ contains all convex combinations of its points. Then, it shows that for any two points $z_1$ and $z_2$ in $S$, their convex combination $tz_1 + (1-t)z_2$ (where $0 \le t \le 1$) is also in $S$. This directly satisfies the definition of a convex set from the previous slide, thus proving that $S$ is convex. The underlining highlights the key steps and conclusions of the proof. The notation "pf" indicates "proof," and the double-headed arrow indicates the "if and only if" nature of the theorem. The term "conv. comb." is an abbreviation for "convex combination." The context of the course (Linear Programming) is crucial for understanding the significance of convex sets in optimization problems, specifically in characterizing feasible regions.

\underline{\text{Thm 10.1}} \quad S \text{ is convex } \iff \\
\text{it contains all conv. comb. of points in } S \\
pf \quad \implies \\
\underline{\text{Suppose } S \text{ is convex}} \\
n=2: \quad z_1, z_2 \in S \implies t_1 z_1 + t_2 z_2 \in S, \quad t_1, t_2 \ge 0 \\
\quad t_1 + t_2 = 1 \\
n=3: \quad z_1, z_2, z_3 \in S \implies t_1 z_1 + t_2 z_2 + t_3 z_3 = (t_1 + t_2) \left( \frac{t_1}{t_1 + t_2} z_1 + \frac{t_2}{t_1 + t_2} z_2 \right) + t_3 z_3 \\
t_1 + t_2 + t_3 = 1 \\
t_1 + t_2 \ge 0, \quad t_3 \ge 0 \\
\implies t_1 z_1 + t_2 z_2 + t_3 z_3 \in S

Proof outline.

Proof for n=3.

3.description: This slide completes the proof of Theorem 10.1, demonstrating that if a set $S$ is convex, then it contains all convex combinations of its points.  The proof uses induction. The base case ($n=2$) is shown: if $z_1, z_2 \in S$, then any convex combination $t_1z_1 + t_2z_2$ (with $t_1, t_2 \ge 0$ and $t_1 + t_2 = 1$) is also in $S$ by the definition of convexity. The inductive step ($n=3$) is then demonstrated. It shows that if $z_1, z_2, z_3 \in S$, then a convex combination $t_1z_1 + t_2z_2 + t_3z_3$ can be rewritten as a convex combination of a convex combination of $z_1$ and $z_2$ and $z_3$. Since the inner convex combination is in $S$ (by the base case), and the outer convex combination is also in $S$ (by the definition of convexity), the entire expression is in $S$. This inductive argument can be extended to any number of points, completing the proof. The underlining highlights key assumptions and conclusions. The notation "pf" stands for "proof," and "conv. comb." is short for "convex combination." The context of linear programming is crucial because this theorem is fundamental to understanding the properties of feasible regions in linear programming problems, which are often convex sets.  The implication arrow ($\implies$) indicates that the proof is showing that if $S$ is convex, then it contains all convex combinations of its points (one direction of the "if and only if" statement from the previous slide).

1.description: This slide presents two equivalent formulations of a linear program in matrix notation. The title "Simplex in Matrix Notation" is underlined. The first formulation is a standard maximization problem: maximize $f(x) = c^Tx$ subject to $Ax \le b$ and $x \ge 0$, where $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$, and $b \in \mathbb{R}^m$. The second formulation introduces slack variables $w \in \mathbb{R}^m$, rewriting the constraints as $w = b - Ax$ and $x, w \ge 0$.  The equivalence between the two formulations is implied by a curved arrow connecting them.  The context of the course (Linear Programming and Optimization Techniques) suggests that this slide introduces the matrix notation used to represent linear programs, which is essential for understanding the simplex method and other optimization algorithms. The slide likely serves as an introduction to the matrix representation of linear programs before delving into the simplex algorithm.

2.description: This slide shows three equivalent formulations of a linear program in matrix notation. The title "Simplex in Matrix Notation" is underlined. The first formulation is a standard maximization problem: maximize $f(x) = c^Tx$ subject to $Ax \le b$ and $x \ge 0$, where $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$, and $b \in \mathbb{R}^m$. The second formulation introduces slack variables $w \in \mathbb{R}^m$, rewriting the constraints as $w = b - Ax$ and $x, w \ge 0$. The third formulation is similar to the second, but uses different notation, with $\overline{w}$, $\overline{b}$, and $\overline{A}$ representing modified slack variables, right-hand side vector, and constraint matrix, respectively, and includes a constant term $j^T$ in the objective function.  Curved arrows indicate the iterative process of the simplex method, transforming the problem from one formulation to the next. The context of the course (Linear Programming and Optimization Techniques) suggests that this slide illustrates how linear programs are represented in matrix form, which is crucial for understanding the simplex algorithm.  The slide likely serves as a transition to explaining the simplex method's iterative process.

3.description: This slide illustrates the simplex method's iterative process using matrix notation within the context of linear programming. The title "Simplex in Matrix Notation" is underlined.  The slide presents two equivalent formulations of a linear program. The first is a standard maximization problem: maximize $f(x) = c^Tx$ subject to $Ax + w = b$ and $x, w \ge 0$, where $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ are the decision variables, $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is the cost vector, $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ is the constraint matrix, $b \in \mathbb{R}^m$ is the right-hand side vector, and $w \in \mathbb{R}^m$ are the slack variables. This is then represented in matrix form as $\begin{bmatrix} A & I \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ w \end{bmatrix} = b$. The second formulation represents a later iteration of the simplex method, where the objective function and constraints have been modified. The objective function is now $\overline{j} + \overline{c}^T x$, and the constraints are $\overline{A}x + \overline{w} = \overline{b}$, with the same non-negativity constraints. This is also represented in matrix form as $\begin{bmatrix} \overline{A} & I \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ \overline{w} \end{bmatrix} = \overline{b}$. The arrow indicates the iterative nature of the simplex algorithm, transforming the initial problem into a modified one during each iteration. The dimensions of the matrices are explicitly stated. The slide emphasizes the use of matrix notation to represent and solve linear programs efficiently.

3.description: This slide presents the Klee-Minty example (1970), a worst-case scenario for the simplex method in linear programming. The title "Worst Case Example: Klee-Minty (1970)" is underlined.  The example is a linear program formulated as a maximization problem with $n$ variables ($x_j$) and $n$ constraints. The objective function is a weighted sum of the variables $x_j$, subtracted by a weighted sum of parameters $\beta_j$. The constraints are inequalities involving weighted sums of the variables $x_j$ and parameters $\beta_j$. The parameters $\beta_j$ satisfy the condition $1 \ll \beta_1 \ll \beta_2 \ll \dots \ll \beta_n$, indicating a significant difference in magnitude between consecutive $\beta_j$ values.  The slide then highlights the performance of two different pivot rules: the Largest Coefficient Rule, which requires $2^n - 1$ steps (exponential complexity), and the Smallest Coefficient Rule, which requires only $n$ steps (linear complexity).  The underlining emphasizes the contrasting performance of these rules. The context of the course (Linear Programming and Optimization Techniques) is crucial because this example demonstrates that the simplex method's efficiency is highly dependent on the chosen pivot rule and can exhibit exponential time complexity in the worst case, despite its generally good performance in practice.
